title: Spectral Audio Signal Processing — shard 4: Appendices A–H, Bibliography, and Index
access: Full text of the assigned shard was read from Julius O. Smith III's official Stanford CCRMA linked-HTML edition at https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos/sasp/. The cache contains exactly 175 table-of-contents pages beginning with Appendix A (Notation), continuing through Appendices B–H, and ending with the Bibliography and Index. The live pages identify W3K Publishing, 2011, ISBN 978-0-9745607-3-1, and carry a footer updated 2026-06-10. Copyright is retained by Julius O. Smith III; no open-content licence is stated. Compact extracted text, including formulas and code listings, is cached at content/courses/digital-signal-processing/research/texts/jos-s4.txt with a metadata sidecar.
topics: Appendix A — Notation: frequency and time variables, sample interval and rate, DFT/DTFT signal notation, conjugate and phase notation, transform-pair correspondence, and pointwise products.
Appendix B — Continuous Fourier Theorems: radians versus cycles, differentiation and its dual, scaling, shift, modulation, convolution, flips, and the power theorem.
Appendix B — generalized signals and canonical transform pairs: the continuous impulse, Gaussian and rectangular pulses, sinc as an impulse limit, and impulse trains.
Appendix B — Poisson summation and sampling theory: reciprocal impulse-train transforms, time aliasing versus spectral sampling, and spectral replication under continuous-time sampling.
Appendix B — uncertainty: duration and bandwidth defined by second moments, the Gaussian lower bound, a stronger bound for time-limited signals, and absence of an upper bound.
Appendix B — smoothness and roll-off: derivative discontinuities, bounded variation, the Riemann lemma, and aliased high-frequency decay for sampled windows.
Appendix C — probability foundations: distributions, independent events, discrete and continuous random variables, PDFs, and stochastic processes.
Appendix C — stationarity and estimation: expected value, ensemble versus time averaging, mean, unbiased sample mean, variance, and the N−1 sample-variance correction when the mean is estimated.
Appendix C — correlation analysis: cross-correlation and cross-power spectral density, autocorrelation and power spectral density, sample estimates, and Hermitian/even symmetries.
Appendix C — white noise: uncorrelated successive samples, impulse autocorrelation, flat PSD, dice generators, and the distinction between independence and uncorrelatedness.
Appendix C — estimator variance: confidence intervals, sample-mean variance, sample-variance variance for Gaussian white noise, and the 1/M benefit of averaging.
Appendix D — Gaussian function properties: Fourier self-similarity, multiplication and convolution closure, fitting a Gaussian by a parabola in the log domain, and infinite flatness.
Appendix D — Gaussian integrals: real and complex Gaussian areas, complex offsets, Fourier transform of a complex Gaussian, and an alternative differential-equation proof.
Appendix D — why Gaussians recur: central-limit behavior of iterated convolutions, the binomial-to-Gaussian limit, and high-order Lagrange interpolation.
Appendix D — entropy: entropy as average coding length and maximum-entropy distributions under finite-support, nonnegative-support/mean, and whole-line/mean/variance constraints.
Appendix D — moments: Gaussian mean, variance, all higher central moments, characteristic functions, the moment theorem, and sums of independent Gaussian random variables.
Appendix E — auditory frequency scales: Bark critical-band rate, ERB scale, published band edges/centers, interpretation as continuous auditory resolution, and sampling-rate extrapolation.
Appendix E — bilinear frequency warping: first-order conformal/allpass maps of the unit circle, coefficient rho, inverse map, and order preservation.
Appendix E — optimal Bark warping: arc, chord, and equation errors; Chebyshev, least-squares, weighted equation-error, and arctangent approximations.
Appendix E — relative bandwidth-mapping error: map slope as critical bandwidth, perceptual significance of 18–21 percent Bark-scale errors, and listener variability.
Appendix E — audio filter design: warp the desired response, design on the perceptual axis, unwarp without increasing filter order, and compare direct versus Bark-weighted Prony fits.
Appendix E — ERB warping: analytic ERB bandwidth/rate formulas, comparison with Bark critical bands, larger systematic first-order-map errors, and optimized arctangent coefficients.
Appendix E — improvement directions: application-specific frequency weighting and cochlear place-based scales.

Appendix F — spectrum-analysis code: Blackman-window zero-phase padding, a direct DPSS eigenvector implementation, peak finding, three-point quadratic interpolation, and zero-padding-factor estimation.
Appendix F — measured oboe analysis: estimate pitch, choose durations in periods, compare rectangular/Hamming/Blackman windows, and enforce at least 5× zero padding.
Appendix F — STFT code: analysis frame construction, zero-phase FFT buffers, spectrogram display, inverse FFT frame rotation, overlap-add reconstruction, and COLA testing.
Appendix F — phase and spectral resampling: phase unwrapping by 2π correction and nonparametric ideal spectral interpolation.
Appendix F — fundamental-frequency estimation: peak detection, partial spacing, harmonic-number assignment, least-squares harmonic regression, and a missing-fundamental test.
Appendix G — origins of spectral modeling: Bernoulli's modal superposition, Euler/d'Alembert debates, pre-Fourier pulse-train theories, and Helmholtz's ear-as-spectrum-analyzer model.
Appendix G — electromechanical synthesis: Cahill's Telharmonium rheotomes, Hammond tone wheels, and hand-drawn photographic film soundtracks.
Appendix G — speech coders: Dudley's ten-band channel vocoder, source-filter buzz/hiss model, formant vocoder, manually performed Voder, and the emergence of phase vocoders.
Appendix G — additive/sinusoidal synthesis: oscillator banks, inverse-FFT synthesis, main-lobe placement, chirplet synthesis, raw spectral-peak modeling, wavetables, and group-additive methods.
Appendix G — FM synthesis: elementary carrier/modulator model, Bessel-distributed sidebands, amplitude-dependent brass brightness, compact formant groups for voice, and Yamaha commercialization.
Appendix G — phase-vocoder parameterization: instantaneous amplitude, phase, frequency deviation, analytic signals, baseband channels, envelope compression, and one-sinusoid-per-channel limitations.

Appendix G — spectral modeling synthesis: peak-adaptive sinusoidal models, IFFT synthesis, sines+noise residual models, multiresolution analysis, explicit transient models, and time-frequency reassignment.
Appendix G — perceptual coding and future prospects: tones/noises/attacks as a compact perceptual basis, masking-driven bit allocation, MPEG milestones, and sparse auditory representations.
Appendix H — PARSHL overview: 1985 inharmonic phase-vocoder for piano, prominent STFT peak tracking, amplitude/frequency/phase trajectories, modifications, and additive or overlap-add resynthesis.
Appendix H — analysis details: hop-size/COLA and aliasing criteria, zero-phase buffer filling, 2× or greater FFT padding, log-magnitude parabolic interpolation, and peak removal.
Appendix H — peak matching: nearest-frequency assignment with maximum-change limits, recursive conflict resolution, start/stop/revive behavior, and oscillator allocation.

Appendix H — modifications and synthesis: time scaling, pitch/formant separation, cross-synthesis, time-alias monitoring, linear amplitude interpolation, cubic phase interpolation, and magnitude-only resynthesis.
Appendix H — preprocessing and applications: perceptual or analytic equalization, noise-floor flattening, reverse-time analysis, hybrid synthesis, phase-matched splicing, and data reduction.

Appendix H — complete SAIL software listing: original 1985 implementation, command interface, window creation, peak finder, partial tracker, oscillator mapping, wavetable synthesis, filtering, overlap-add, and file I/O.

Bibliography — 308 numbered sources spanning Fourier analysis, DSP, psychoacoustics, filter banks, spectral estimation, computer music, synthesis, coding, and the primary historical papers cited in the appendices.
Index — detailed term-to-section map for the complete online book, including cross-references and alternate terminology.
key_results: Appendix A, Frequency and Time: ω is rad/s, f is Hz with ω=2πf; T is the sample interval, fs=1/T, and tn=nT.
Appendix A, Signal/Fourier Notation: x∈C^N maps by the N-point DFT to X∈C^N; pointwise spectral multiplication is denoted XY and implemented as elementwise multiplication.
Appendix B, Differentiation: dx/dt transforms to jωX(ω), while -jtx(t) transforms to dX/dω.
Appendix B, Scaling: x(t/α) transforms to |α|X(αω); stretching time squeezes frequency and scales amplitude.
Appendix B, Shift and Modulation: x(t−τ) transforms to e^{-jωτ}X(ω), while x(t)e^{jνt} transforms to X(ω−ν).
Appendix B, Convolution/Power: time convolution transforms to spectral multiplication, and the time-domain inner product equals the properly normalized spectral inner product.
Appendix B, Impulse: the Dirac impulse is a generalized function characterized by unit area and the sifting property; it is the limit of any unit-area pulse shrinking to zero width.
Appendix B, Rect/sinc pair: a width-τ rectangular pulse transforms to τ sinc(fτ), and τ sinc(τf) converges distributionally to δ(f) as τ grows.
Appendix B, impulse trains: the normalized shah is self-Fourier; an impulse train spaced P seconds transforms to an impulse train spaced 1/P Hz with areas scaled by 1/P.
Appendix B, Poisson summation: periodic aliasing of w(t) with period R equals the inverse Fourier series formed from samples W(k/R)/R, making spectral sampling and time aliasing dual.
Appendix B, continuous sampling: multiplying x(t) by a T-spaced impulse train produces fs-scaled spectral replicas X(f−kfs); bandlimiting below fs/2 prevents overlap.
Appendix B, uncertainty: with duration and bandwidth defined as normalized second moments, Δt·Δω≥1/2, with equality only for a Gaussian.
Appendix B, time-limited bound: if x(t)=0 outside an interval of duration Δt, then Δt·Δω≥π under the appendix's second-moment bandwidth definition.
Appendix B, no upper uncertainty bound: an allpass filter can preserve bandwidth while extending duration arbitrarily.

Appendix B, Riemann lemma: if derivatives through order n have bounded variation, W(ω)=O(1/ω^{n+1}); practically, n smooth derivatives imply about -6(n+1) dB/octave roll-off until discrete-time aliasing flattens the envelope near Nyquist.
Appendix C, sample mean: for a stationary process, the N-sample average is an unbiased estimator of the true mean.
Appendix C, sample variance: division by N is unbiased when the true mean is known; replacing it by the sample mean requires division by N−1.
Appendix C, correlation spectra: DTFT{rxy} is the cross-PSD, DTFT{rx} is the PSD, and a real process has real-even autocorrelation and PSD.
Appendix C, white noise: whiteness requires zero correlation at nonzero lags, not a particular amplitude distribution; its autocorrelation is σ²δ(m) and its PSD is flat.
Appendix C, independence: independent zero-mean samples are uncorrelated; for jointly Gaussian variables, uncorrelatedness also implies independence.
Appendix C, averaging gain: the variance of an M-sample mean of uncorrelated samples is σ²/M.
Appendix C, variance-estimator variance: for zero-mean Gaussian white noise, Var(sample variance)=2σ⁴/M, again falling as 1/M.
Appendix D, Gaussian transform: (1/(σ√(2π)))e^{-t²/(2σ²)} transforms to e^{-ω²/[2(1/σ)²]}; narrowing in one domain widens reciprocally in the other.
Appendix D, closure: products and convolutions of Gaussians remain Gaussian; the product variance is the reciprocal-sum combination σ1²σ2²/(σ1²+σ2²).
Appendix D, complex Gaussian integral: for Re(p)>0, ∫e^{-pt²}dt=√(π/p), and a complex shift does not change the integral.
Appendix D, complex Gaussian transform: e^{-pt²} transforms to √(π/p)e^{-ω²/(4p)} for Re(p)>0, covering Gaussian-windowed chirps.

Appendix D, Gaussian fitting: taking a logarithm converts a Gaussian peak to a parabola; weighted least squares should weight inverse noise variance, with data-amplitude weighting reported as useful in practice.
Appendix D, central-limit mechanism: repeated convolution raises a smooth-tipped characteristic function approximately (1−αω²)^N≈e^{-Nαω²}, explaining convergence toward a Gaussian.

Appendix D, entropy: h(p)=E[log2(1/p(x))] is the average ideal code length; a fair random bit has entropy 1 bit, while probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 yield 0.81128 bits and about 19 percent compressibility.

Appendix D, maximum entropy: the uniform distribution maximizes entropy on a fixed finite interval, the exponential maximizes it on [0,∞) for fixed mean, and the Gaussian maximizes it on the real line for fixed mean and variance.
Appendix D, Gaussian moments: odd central moments vanish and even moments are (n−1)!!σ^n, giving m4=3σ⁴, m6=15σ⁶, and m8=105σ⁸.
Appendix D, moment theorem: E{x^n}=(1/j^n)d^nΦ/dω^n evaluated at zero, where Φ is the characteristic function.
Appendix E, Bark scale: 24 published critical bands span 0 to 15.5 kHz; one Bark is one critical bandwidth, and the inverse mapping should be optimized so errors are measured perceptually in Barks.
Appendix E, bilinear map: z=(ζ+ρ)/(1+ρζ) maps the unit circle to itself, fixes DC and Nyquist, has inverse coefficient -ρ, and preserves filter order because the substitution is first order.

Appendix E, Bark fit quality: at 31 kHz, optimal Chebyshev, least-squares, and weighted equation-error maps are nearly identical; L2 is within 0.04 Bark of L∞, below typical critical-band measurement uncertainty.

Appendix E, Bark errors: at 31 kHz, peak mapping error is about 0.64 Bark for Chebyshev and 0.67 Bark for least squares; relative bandwidth-mapping error is about 18–20 percent when optimized for slope.

Appendix E, perceptual significance: measured auditory-filter bandwidths vary widely across listeners, so a 20 percent worst-case mapping error may be detectable by expert listeners but lies inside empirical population variation.
Appendix E, Bark coefficient shortcut: with fs in kHz, rho≈1.0674√[(2/π)atan(0.06583fs)]−0.1916 closely approximates the optimal Chebyshev map and generally adds under 0.1 Bark peak error.

Appendix E, filter-design result: prewarping a desired response to Bark, fitting there, and unwarping yields a same-order filter that allocates approximation accuracy more evenly per critical band; the 12th-order example fits below 4 kHz much better than an unwarped fit.
Appendix E, ERB formulas: ERB(f)=0.108f+24.7 Hz and ERBS(f)=21.4log10(0.00437f+1); ERB approaches about 11 percent of center frequency at high frequencies and about 25 Hz at low frequencies.

Appendix E, ERB limitation: at 31 kHz a first-order map has about 1.9 Bark peak error and over 60 percent peak relative-bandwidth error—roughly three times the Bark case—because it cannot stretch low frequencies enough.
Appendix F, DPSS code: build the sampled-sinc Toeplitz matrix, take the eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue, and normalize its peak to obtain the maximum-concentration window.
Appendix F, quadratic interpolation: three uniform samples around a maximum determine offset p=(y+1−y−1)/[2(2y0−y+1−y−1)], peak height, and curvature.

Appendix F, STFT reconstruction test: a properly normalized COLA Hamming window with 50 percent hop reconstructs the chirp example to relative L2 error around 8×10^-16 for both odd and even window lengths.

Appendix F, fundamental estimation: after interpolating spectral peaks, assign harmonic numbers and solve a one-parameter least-squares regression; the test estimates 440 Hz as 439.99 Hz with all harmonics and 437.50 Hz after notching out the fundamental.

Appendix G, vocoder architecture: Dudley's original system analyzed ten bands over 250–3000 Hz, sent their amplitude envelopes plus F0/voicing, and resynthesized with buzz or hiss through matching filters.

Appendix G, phase vocoder: adding complex channel phase removes explicit pitch tracking because phase modulation fine-tunes a sinusoid within its band, but good compression still assumes no more than one sinusoid per channel.

Appendix G, IFFT synthesis: writing whole window-transform main lobes rather than isolated FFT bins creates time-shaped sinusoidal envelopes; chirp-rate-indexed main lobes extend this to within-frame frequency sweeps.
Appendix G, FM spectra: kth sideband amplitude is proportional to Jk(beta); increasing modulation index moves power into more sidebands and perceptually brightens the tone.

Appendix G, FM voice compression: three FM carrier/modulator pairs can approximate three vowel formant groups using six oscillators, versus as many as about 200 additive oscillators for a 100 Hz voice extending to 20 kHz.

Appendix G, envelope compression: slowly varying tonal amplitude/frequency envelopes historically reached roughly 100:1 compression; critical downsampling of N filter-bank channels by N returns one parameter sample per input sample overall.

Appendix G, modern sinusoidal modeling: replacing the uniform vocoder bank by an STFT peak-adaptive sparse bank avoids empty channels and tracks inharmonic partials; it can be understood as a pruned phase vocoder.

Appendix G, sines+noise+transients: sinusoids compactly represent tonal components, filtered white noise represents the steady residual, and explicit transient segments preserve attacks without hundreds of partials.

Appendix G, perceptual sparsity: a tones/noises/attacks model achieved AAC-comparable quality around 32 kbps while remaining amenable to time and frequency transformations; the text reports over 90 percent of typical audio information can often be removed inaudibly.

Appendix H, hop-size criterion: COLA is conservative and guarantees equal weighting, while modified-STFT alias control instead requires the folding frequency fs/(2R) to exceed the window cutoff; resulting overlaps are 50 percent rectangular, 75 percent Hann/Hamming, and about 83 percent Blackman.
Appendix H, buffer rule: a zero-centered odd window stores zero and positive times first, negative times at the buffer end, and all zero padding in the middle.

Appendix H, peak accuracy: brute-force bin selection needs roughly 1000× padding for 0.1-percent peak-position accuracy, while three-bin parabolic interpolation reaches that target with about 5× padding for a rectangular window.
Appendix H, log-domain interpolation: fitting the top three samples in dB gives empirical frequency estimates about twice as accurate as fitting linear magnitude; p=0.5(α−γ)/(α−2β+γ).

Appendix H, track assignment: each prior track claims the nearest current peak within a frequency-dependent limit; conflicts go to the closer track recursively, unmatched tracks ramp down, and unused peaks start new zero-ramped tracks.

Appendix H, legal modifications: spectral multiplication is safe if zero padding accommodates the corresponding time convolution; inverse-transform the modification and monitor buffer-midpoint energy to expose time-alias risk.

Appendix H, sinusoidal synthesis: amplitude is linearly interpolated, while endpoint phase and frequency constraints require a cubic phase polynomial with the cycle count chosen for maximum smoothness.
Appendix H, reverse analysis: reversing a sound lets the stable decay establish important tracks before the noisy attack, preventing the fixed oscillator pool from being consumed by transient peaks.

Appendix H, perceptual result: phase-free synthesis can sound equivalent in some cases despite a visibly different waveform, but phase becomes crucial for speech, modifications, and inaudible splicing of sampled attacks to modeled steady states.

Appendix H, extreme reduction: PARSHL reportedly preserved intelligible speech using only the three strongest sinusoidal components, motivating a hypothesis of higher-level spectral-feature dominance beyond critical-band masking.
pedagogy: These appendices function as a layered reference and laboratory. Appendices A and B establish conventions and prove the continuous-time results that the main chapters use without interruption. Appendix C introduces only the probability needed for practical noise analysis, consistently moving from a coin or dice example to an estimator formula. Appendix D is a sustained mathematical case study: the Gaussian is approached through Fourier duality, closure, contour integration, central-limit behavior, entropy, and moments, with multiple proofs reinforcing the same structure. Appendix E is research-style engineering exposition: psychoacoustic data motivate an approximation family, several norms are compared quantitatively, error significance is judged against listener variability, and a measured filter-fit example closes the loop. Appendix F is executable pedagogy—complete MATLAB/Octave functions expose exact indexing, padding, peak fitting, STFT inversion, and regression details. Appendix G tells the technical history chronologically, connecting devices and algorithms to the signal models they embody. Appendix H republishes a detailed original implementation paper and full 1985 SAIL source, moving step by step from STFT parameters through tracking and resynthesis while openly recording tradeoffs and failure modes. The appendices assume calculus, complex variables, Fourier analysis, linear algebra, elementary DSP, and programming fluency; Appendix C supplies a compact probability refresher. Exercises appear in the theorem appendices, but the dominant learning pattern is derivation followed by numerical rule, historical or measured example, and implementable code.

gems: Appendix B, Uncertainty Principle: an allpass filter gives the shortest possible proof that time-bandwidth product has no upper bound—it changes no magnitude bandwidth but can extend duration without limit.
Appendix B, Smoothness and Roll-Off: the impulse-to-step-to-ramp ladder turns each time integration into one extra factor 1/(jω), making the -6 dB/octave per smooth derivative rule almost visual.

Appendix C, Random Variables: two dice turn two discrete uniform distributions into a triangular distribution by convolution, connecting an elementary probability experiment directly to an essential DSP operation.

Appendix C, White Noise with Dice: one die and two dice generate different amplitude histograms, yet both sequences are white if rolls are independent—a sharp separation of spectrum from marginal distribution.

Appendix C, Stationarity: 20 ms is offered as a typical frequency-independent audio frame over which statistics can be treated as approximately stationary; multiresolution frames instead span several center-frequency periods.
Appendix C, Estimator Variance: averaging M independent observations cuts variance by M, while Gaussian variance estimation costs twice the normalized variance, 2σ⁴/M.

Appendix D, Infinite Flatness: e^{-1/t²} has every derivative zero at t=0 yet is nonzero nearby, a striking counterexample to the intuition that an all-order Taylor series must recover a smooth function.
Appendix D, Random Bits: moving from a fair bit to probabilities 1/4 and 3/4 lowers entropy from 1 to 0.81128 bits, making the abstract entropy integral a concrete 19-percent compression opportunity.
Appendix D, Why Gaussian: the tiny local approximation 1−αω², raised by repeated convolution to the Nth power, becomes e^{-Nαω²}; the bell curve emerges from a one-line Fourier-domain limit.
Appendix D, Binomial Link: the bottom row of Pascal's triangle tends to a sampled Gaussian, so high-order Lagrange interpolation tends toward Gaussian-windowed sinc interpolation.

Appendix E, Psychoacoustic Equivalence: least-squares Bark warping lies within 0.04 Bark of the minimax optimum, below typical critical-band experimental uncertainty, so a closed-form practical map is as meaningful as the formal optimum.

Appendix E, Listener Variability: auditory-filter bandwidths around 2 kHz ranged roughly 230–410 Hz in one cohort and -33 to +65 percent in another, grounding a 20-percent mapping error in actual human variation.
Appendix E, Same-Order Perceptual Design: a first-order allpass warp lets a 12th-order filter spend accuracy per Bark and then unwarp while remaining 12th order.
Appendix E, Bark versus ERB: the same elegant first-order map is excellent for Bark but roughly three times worse for ERB, because ERB continues narrowing at low frequencies while Bark levels off.

Appendix F, Machine-Precision STFT: the short test program achieves roughly 8×10^-16 relative reconstruction error, giving learners a concrete pass/fail target for zero-phase indexing and COLA normalization.
Appendix F, Missing Fundamental: the harmonic-regression estimator returns 439.99 Hz for a 440 Hz tone and still returns 437.50 Hz after the 440 Hz component itself is removed.

Appendix G, Bernoulli Debate: 18th-century resistance to sinusoidal superposition included what would now be called intermodulation distortion—an intuitive but misplaced physical objection that took modern convergence theory to settle.

Appendix G, Voder Performance: ten fingers controlled band gains, a foot pedal controlled pitch, a wrist bar selected buzz or hiss, and about a year of training was needed to perform intelligible speech.

Appendix G, Vocoder Compression: the original ten-band 250–3000 Hz analysis reduced speech to F0/voicing plus ten slowly changing envelopes, accepting an 'electrical accent' for a much smaller transmission bandwidth.

Appendix G, FM Brass: Risset's observation that brass spectra brighten with amplitude led Chowning to make FM index proportional to the amplitude envelope—a measured acoustic regularity translated into one control connection.
Appendix G, FM Voice: six oscillators arranged as three FM pairs can approximate three formants that brute-force additive synthesis might represent with roughly 200 oscillators.
Appendix G, Model Progression: phase vocoder to sparse sinusoids to sines+noise to sines+noise+transients is presented as a sequence of fixing empty channels, noisy residuals, and costly attacks.

Appendix G, Sparse Brain Hypothesis: the observation that most primary auditory-cortex neurons are silent most of the time is used to ask what higher-level sparse representation follows the cochlea's spectrogram.
Appendix H, Padding Economics: 0.1-percent peak precision would require about 1000× zero padding by bin selection alone, but only about 5× when followed by a three-bin parabolic fit.

Appendix H, dB Interpolation: the original authors found parabolic peak-frequency interpolation in dB about twice as accurate as interpolation in linear magnitude and explicitly leave the optimal magnitude compression as an open question.
Appendix H, Reverse the Sound: analyzing decay-to-attack lets stable piano partials claim the finite oscillator pool before the noisy onset, a wonderfully simple algorithmic use of time reversal.

Appendix H, Be Gentle in Frequency: the practical warning links abrupt spectral edits to long time-domain filters, insufficient padding, and audible time aliasing; inspecting the inverse FFT of the modification makes the risk measurable.

Appendix H, Phase and Perception: magnitude-only synthesis may sound similar while looking radically different, yet phase is decisive for speech, transformations, and seamless attachment of real attacks to modeled sustains.

Appendix H, Three-Sine Speech: intelligible speech reportedly survives reduction to only the three strongest sinusoidal components, motivating the analogy between spectral peaks and the outlines that let vision recognize an object.

Appendix H, Living Source Artifact: the full 1985 SAIL implementation preserves not just algorithms but design diary comments about competing track-allocation strategies, making it unusually valuable as engineering history.

Bibliography: the back matter supplies 308 primary and secondary references, including the original papers behind Welch estimation, phase vocoding, reassignment, FM, sinusoidal modeling, and perfect-reconstruction filter banks.
